Hospital-acquired Clostridium difficile (C. difficile) is a particularly challenging bacteria that can cause severe diarrhea and death.
In the US alone, C. difficile is estimated to lead to more than 14,500 deaths and result in more than $1.1 billion in costs per year.
The high-speed visualizations were recorded at 1000 to 2000 frames per second.
The visualizations captured large quantities of both large and small droplets being ejected during the flushing process.
Large droplets would settle quickly and contaminate surfaces, while smaller droplets could remain suspended in the air.
The smaller droplets could carry C. difficile spores and other pathogens.
Modern hospital toilets in North America do not have lids and are cleared using high-flow rate flushes.
Previous research by Best et al. (2012) reported finding C. difficile spores in the air an hour after flushing.
Fluid dynamics is playing an increasingly important role in understanding the transmission of a variety of diseases.
The authors' high-speed visualizations show that current hospital flushing practices can lead to the suspension and recirculation of tenacious potential pathogens.
The authors conclude that the current flushing practices may be aggravating the problem of hospital-acquired infections rather than alleviating it.
The authors plan to publish their full results on the fluid fragmentation dynamics of flush-induced droplet ejecta in a separate publication.
The research presented in this paper is the first step in a larger effort to understand and address the problem of air contamination from hospital toilets.
